# Technique — RESPx re-strobing: more copies a scanline, and how many depends on the spacing

**Goal:** put more shaped slots on one scanline than NUSIZ alone gives. Two players with three
copies each is six; at the right strobe spacing re-strobing takes one player to eight and two
players to sixteen — both measured, the second one on its own band rather than by doubling the
first. That is the floor under any dense-text kernel (`text12.md`, `text24.md`, `bitmap48.md`).

**Status:** ✅ measured and CI-locked. Fixture `roms/litmus/litmus_restrobe.asm` (generated by
`scripts/gen_litmus_restrobe.py`); grading `internal/emu/restrobe_test.go`.
**Primary source, added 2026-09-04: US Patent 4,623,147**, "Process for displaying a plurality of
objects on a video screen" — Mark S. Ackerman and Glenn Parker, GCC Technologies, filed 1983-09-20,
granted 1986-11-18. The people who invented this describe it **twenty-eight years** before the post
below: writing a new NUSIZ value *during the active scan line, after a reset*, to get copies beyond
the three the register nominally offers, and with timed resets plus consecutive GRP0/GRP1 loads, up
to four graphically distinct high-resolution objects on one line. The invariant our rule table exists
to pin down is stated there in one clause: the position counters are *"clocked continuously during
the unblanked portion of every horizontal line"*, and *"each player position counter has three
decodes in addition to the zero crossing decode … controlled by data bits D0, D1, and D2 of the
8-bit number/spacing control registers"*.

**Source:** `reference/atariage/180632-32-character-text-display` records solidcorp's 2011
32-character display and files this mechanism as **candidate ⑨, unverified** — "re-strobe
RESP0/RESP1 several times a line with NUSIZ at three copies close and the copy sequence restarts".
Measured here 2026-08-25, from private `roms/` work that had concluded six shaped slots was a
hardware ceiling and went looking for why; the spacing sweep and the two-player band were added
2026-08-26, after the first version of this doc was found to be generalising from one spacing.

**Cycle convention is this catalogue's:** `c` is the **write cycle** — the last of the three cycles
of `sta RESPx` — and a normal-width player lands at **`x = 3c − 60`** (`sprite-placement.md` rule 1).

**The single-copy case is a different fixture.** `roms/litmus/litmus_resp_edge.asm` already pins
that a mid-line `RESBL` re-emits START (two balls on one line) while `RESPx` does not (one player,
at the last position). Everything below is about a player in a **COPY mode**, which is the case that
fixture does not cover and where the answer is the opposite one.

**And the missiles are a third answer again.** `roms/litmus/litmus_restrobe_objects.asm` sweeps all
of them over width, spacing and k: the ball draws **1 + k** blocks, a MISSILE draws **1** — `RESM0`
and `RESM1` appear nowhere in `litmus_resp_edge`, so that half had never been measured — and a
missile struck inside its own block is EXTENDED past the 8 px its size field allows. So a row of
solid blocks down one line is a ball technique, not a missile one. The table is in
`sprite-placement.md`, under rules 11 and 13.

## The ladder is a function of the SPACING, not a constant

`litmus_restrobe` parks P0 at x=3 with NUSIZ=3 (three copies, sixteen apart) while the screen is
still blank, then each band re-strobes RESP0 k times on ONE picture line, `s` cycles apart, first
strobe at cycle 29. Copies drawn:

| spacing s | k=1 | k=2 | k=3 | k=4 | k=5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| 4 | 4 | — | — | — | — |
| 5 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| 6 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| 7 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| 8 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| 10 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 6 |
| 12 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 9 | — |

(A dash is a schedule the machine cannot build: a gap of exactly one cycle has no filler, and a
store ending past cycle 74 runs out of scanline.)

**Read the rows that disagree with each other.** Only 6, 7 and 8 give the "3 + k" ladder:

- **3 and 5 are FLAT at four.** Every strobe after the first buys nothing at all. Whatever a strobe
  needs in order to be worth a copy, three and five cycles do not supply it.
- **10 climbs and then falls** — 4, 5, 6, 7, then 6 at k=5, because by then the copies are running
  off the right-hand edge rather than being lost to the mechanism.
- **12 climbs FASTER than 3 + k** — 4, 6, 8, 9 — so "net +1 per strobe" is not the law either.

**THE MECHANISM BEHIND THE SPACING DEPENDENCE IS NOT ESTABLISHED HERE.** The table is measured; the
reason one spacing behaves differently from its neighbour is not. Two models were written down and
each is refuted by a row of this same table — "a pending copy draws if it is behind the beam when
the next strobe lands" (at s=8 the new base is behind the beam and still does not draw) and "the new
base is always suppressed" (at s=6 the bases are exactly what draws). Saying so is the point of this
section. The previous version of this file had a mechanism and a sentence reading *"the eight-cycle
spacing in the fixture is not special; any spacing at or above three cycles works"* — confident,
tidy, and false at three of the eight spacings now measured.

## Where the copies land, at the two spacings that differ most

```
s=8, k=5   3  19      43      67      91     115     139  155
s=6, k=5   3  19    45    63    81    99   115   131
```

At **spacing 8** every added copy sits **off** the multiple-of-three grid: a strobe base is `3c − 60`,
always a multiple of three, and what draws is base+16 and base+32, which land at ≡ 1 and ≡ 2. At
**spacing 6** every added copy **is** a multiple of three — 45, 63, 81, 99 — because there it is the
bases themselves that draw.

This matters to any kernel placing letters on a uniform pitch, because a row needs every residue and
only an object's **parked** base is free to be at ≡ 0. Both halves are witnessed by the test, in both
directions: it asserts that spacing 8 produces no multiple of three AND that spacing 6 does. The
first version of this doc stated only the spacing-8 half, and stated it as a law that "binds every
kernel built on this".

**The leading two copies are fixed** at the parked base and base+16, at every spacing in the table.
Only what comes after the first strobe is yours to place.

## Two players: sixteen, measured

The fixture's last band puts both players in NUSIZ=3, parks P0 at x=3 and P1 at x=12, and interleaves
their strobes three cycles apart on a six-cycle step. On one scanline:

```
P0   3  19    45    63    81    99   115   131
P1     12    28    54    72    90   108   124   140
```

**Sixteen objects, sixteen distinct positions.** Two players do not simply add — their strobes share
one 76-cycle line and each is three cycles — so this is a band rather than an arithmetic claim. It is
here because the opening sentence of this doc used to say "two players to sixteen" while only one
player had ever been measured, and the doc's own real-world datapoint below is EIGHT slots a scanline.

Note what sixteen slots does *not* give you: at this schedule the copies sit 9 and 7 pixels apart in
alternation, so **three of the sixteen are clipped to 7 px** by the next object starting. Sixteen
places is not sixteen full-width places.

## What it costs

`203487_36char.bin` (attached to that thread; disassembled here with `cmd/beamtrace`) spends one
scanline like this:

```
cycle  0   RESP0            the line opens with one
      14   GRP0 = $55
      20   GRP1 = $75
      26   GRP0 = $44
      32   GRP0 = $21
      42   GRP1 = $55
      48   GRP1 = $55
      51   RESP0            mid-line
      54   GRP0 = $A4
      57   RESP0            and again
      61   GRP0 = $A8
      67   GRP0 = $AA
      73   HMP1 = $80
```

Nine GRP writes, three strobes, ending at cycle 73 of 76 — **the budget is spent, not merely used.**
The writes sit six cycles apart, which is `lda zp` (3) plus `sta GRPx` (3); the 3–3–3 burst in the
middle is stores from registers already loaded. Every byte is a pair of nibbles (`$77` = 7,7;
`$E4` = E,4), so a slot is two characters at 4 px.

**Count the slots on the screen rather than the writes in the listing.** Decomposing two adjacent
scanlines of that ROM (65 and 66, `emu.DecomposeRow`):

```
line 65 slots:    28   44   60   76   92  100  116  132
line 66 slots: 20   36   52   68   84       108  124  140
union        : 20 28 36 44 52 60 68 76 84 92 100 108 116 124 132 140   -- 16 slots, 8 apart
```

**Eight slots a scanline = sixteen characters; the thirty-two of the thread's title are TWO
scanlines interleaved**, a venetian blind, and 128 px / 32 characters is exactly the 4 px the
nibbles say. Nine writes did not mean nine drawn slots, and reading the count off the listing gave
eighteen and thirty-six here until the pixels were counted.

**What the blind does NOT cost is a blank line.** All eleven scanlines of each text row draw; the
alternation is between odd and even COLUMNS, not between drawing and repositioning, because the
re-strobes rebuild the positions inside the drawing line itself. What it does cost is density: each
character appears on every other scanline, which is why the glyphs read as dotted.

**The arithmetic that decides whether a design fits:** slots come from re-strobing, but bytes come
from the line's cycles. At six cycles a write a line affords about ten writes, and how many letters
that is depends entirely on how many fit in a byte — two 4 px letters to a byte is twenty, one 8 px
letter to a byte is ten. Widening the letter costs count at exactly that rate, and no amount of
re-strobing changes it.

## Traps

- **Do not pick a strobe spacing without measuring that spacing.** Three of the eight in the table
  above do not give the published ladder, and two of those three give nothing at all after the first
  strobe. The fixture sweeps s because a ladder measured at one spacing cannot tell a law from a
  coincidence — the same rule `check_instruments.py` enforces on measurement functions.
- **Do not read the glyph bytes from a table indexed by Y.** `lda abs,y` is four cycles against
  three for `lda zp`, and at ten writes a line that is the difference between 72 and 82 of 76. Dense
  text kernels compose their bytes into RAM during VBLANK and the kernel only streams them — which
  is why `cmd/dissect` finds no ROM match for any graphics stream in `36char.bin`.
- **Do not strobe RESxx at cycle 0 or cycle 3 after HMOVE.** The strobe races HMOVE's extra clock
  pulses and the object lands one pixel differently on different consoles; cycles 1 and 2 are safe
  (`reference/atariage/311795-576-1008-characters`, alex_79 and jetsetilly — the race is modelled in
  Gopher2600).
- **A strobe in horizontal blank behaves differently from a mid-line one**, and the fixture shows
  both: its re-park strobe (write cycle 21, beam still at −5) leaves the OLD base's copies on the
  line it runs on, so a kernel cannot park and use the new position on the same scanline. That line
  is not a baseline, and the grader takes the line AFTER it as the sentinel for exactly this reason.
- **Three probes in the originating work concluded a strobe never draws on its own line**, and all
  three were built the same wrong way: the claim is about a copy SEQUENCE restarting, and each of
  them measured a player with ONE copy, where "the first copy" and "the only copy" are the same
  thing and rule 8 eats it. **Measure the mechanism's own precondition.** `litmus_resp_edge` had
  already pinned the single-copy answer; nothing here contradicts it.

## The ball is the one object this technique does not reach

Re-strobing multiplies **players and missiles**. The **ball cannot be replicated horizontally** — it is,
in the source's words, a degraded missile: same 1-clock body, no NUSIZ copies to strobe against
〔190154:40〕. So a layout that needs four small movers on one line gets them from BL + M0 + M1 plus
copies of the missiles, never from copies of the ball.

The solver already encodes this and the catalogue did not say it: `internal/place/place.go:194-197`
offers players and missiles the full pattern set `{0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x06}` and gives the
ball `{0x00}` alone. Written down 2026-09-03, after an audit found the constraint living only in code.
